paragraphs: The paper studies recommendation systems in which content providers act strategically. This makes recommendation a problem involving incentives as well as selecting content: the system must account for providers who make choices within it. The authors use game theory to examine two requirements for such systems, fairness and stability, and show that traditional approaches do not satisfy these requirements.

Their proposed solution is the Shapley mediator, a mechanism for handling recommendations in this strategic setting. The central result is that it satisfies both the fairness and stability requirements established in the paper. These properties are considered together, so the contribution addresses their compatibility within one recommendation mechanism.

The authors also show that the mediator runs in linear time and is the unique economically efficient mechanism satisfying these properties. This uniqueness claim concerns the paper's particular requirements and setting. The findings connect a computationally efficient recommendation rule with formal guarantees about how a system treats strategic providers and remains stable.
neurips-2018-a-game-theoretic-approach-t.tldr: The Shapley mediator provides a linear-time recommendation mechanism with fairness, stability, and a uniqueness guarantee among economically efficient mechanisms.

paragraphs: A neural classifier can assign high confidence to inputs that differ substantially from its training data, including adversarial inputs. This paper proposes a detection method applicable to any pretrained neural classifier with a softmax output. It uses the network's internal features to assess whether an input resembles the examples associated with a known class.

The method models class-conditional feature distributions as Gaussian distributions, using features from both lower and upper levels of the network. It then derives a confidence score from Mahalanobis distance. This gives the detection rule a statistical reference based on class-specific feature distributions, rather than relying only on the classifier's output confidence.

In the reported experiments, the method achieves state-of-the-art performance for detecting both out-of-distribution and adversarial examples. The authors also observe greater robustness when training labels are noisy or examples are scarce. A further application concerns class-incremental learning: the classification rule can incorporate new classes associated with detected unfamiliar samples without additional training of the deep model.
neurips-2018-a-simple-unified-framework-.tldr: A Gaussian model of pretrained network features supplies a Mahalanobis confidence score that detects unfamiliar and adversarial inputs effectively in experiments.

paragraphs: Large extensive-form games are often solved by first constructing a smaller abstraction. The difficult question is how well a strategy computed in that simplified game performs in the original. Earlier theoretical results addressed separate kinds of abstraction and solution concepts under particular structural assumptions, leaving their guarantees fragmented.

This paper develops a common framework that expresses the abstraction types and solution concepts covered by previous guaranteed approaches while retaining comparable quality bounds. It also gives an exact decomposition of abstraction error for a broader class of games. That decomposition is ex post: its value depends on the particular strategy selected, rather than providing a strategy-independent assessment in advance.

Using this decomposition and somewhat weaker assumptions, the authors generalize earlier bounds. Counterexamples show that assumptions of this kind are necessary for some games. They additionally establish the first bounds for transferring approximate Nash equilibria from abstractions to original games, addressing situations where exact solutions are too costly. The results apply to general-sum games with any number of players.
neurips-2018-a-unified-framework-for-ext.tldr: A unified framework bounds the errors of game abstractions, including how approximate Nash equilibria perform when transferred to the original game.

paragraphs: The paper learns a compact dynamical system from high-dimensional sequences such as video. The aim is to represent how a sequence evolves using a low-dimensional latent state. This learned state and its dynamics provide a basis for predicting future states and planning, linking representation learning with decisions about future evolution.

The inference procedure combines a neural inference network with a refinement process. Together, they produce samples from a variational distribution conditioned on an observed sequence. The authors exploit a connection between control and inference, using path-integral control to approximately solve an inference problem that is otherwise intractable. The refinement therefore forms part of the method for obtaining the latent representation.

The paper also introduces an efficient planning method that uses the learned latent dynamics. Numerical experiments show tighter lower bounds for statistical learning of sequential data when using the proposed inference procedure. This supports the approach as a way to improve the variational learning objective while producing a dynamical model that can also support prediction and planning.
neurips-2018-adaptive-path-integral-auto.tldr: Path-integral control refines variational inference to learn compact dynamics from sequences and support prediction and planning.

paragraphs: Spectral estimation asks how a signal's energy is distributed across frequencies. With incomplete or noisy observations, the task involves uncertainty about the spectrum as well as estimating its shape. This paper treats that uncertainty as part of the estimation problem by building a joint probabilistic model of the signal, its observations, and its spectrum.

The approach assumes a Gaussian process prior over the signal. Under that assumption, the authors use Bayes' rule to derive an analytic posterior distribution for the spectrum given the observations. The result describes uncertainty about spectral content rather than reducing the output to a single estimate. The model also supplies a functional representation of the power spectral density that can be optimized efficiently.

The authors connect their method theoretically to Lomb-Scargle estimation, showing that it is an infinite-dimensional variant of that approach. They also compare it with previous methods through three experiments. The contribution combines this connection to an existing estimator with a probabilistic treatment designed for partial, noisy signal measurements.
neurips-2018-bayesian-nonparametric-spec.tldr: A Gaussian-process model yields an analytic posterior over a signal's spectrum, explicitly representing uncertainty from partial and noisy observations.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover clusters in random bipartite graphs. Its focus is cluster size: small groups can be difficult to identify, and the previous algorithms described in the abstract could only recover clusters at least on the order of the square root of the number of vertices. The authors seek to reach substantially smaller groups.

They propose a simple algorithm with two steps and prove that it can find tiny clusters of size O(n^ε), where n is the graph's number of vertices and ε is positive. For small positive exponents, this reaches sizes below the square-root scale. The guarantee concerns the random bipartite graph setting studied in the paper.

Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data show recovery of extremely small clusters even with substantial destructive noise. These observations complement the theoretical size result by examining noisy data. The contribution is therefore both a stronger provable reach for small clusters in the stated setting and empirical evidence that the algorithm can recover small groups under noise.
neurips-2018-bipartite-stochastic-block-.tldr: A two-step algorithm provably recovers tiny clusters in random bipartite graphs and finds very small noisy clusters in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper investigates algorithms that minimize a sum of n smooth functions. Many standard methods construct updates from the span of component gradients selected independently at random. The authors identify this span assumption as a source of computational limits in the big-data regime, where the condition number κ is O(n).

Under that restriction, reaching accuracy ε requires at least n ln(1/ε) iterations in the stated analysis. SVRG and SARAH combine full-gradient information with component gradients, placing them outside this assumption. The paper shows that modifications of these methods can exploit that difference to achieve a speedup whose size depends on the relationship between n and κ.

For accuracy ε = 1/n^α and condition number κ = n^β, with α and β between zero and one, modified SVRG needs O(n) iterations, compared with O(n ln(n)) for methods subject to the span assumption. Lower bounds establish the optimality of the speedup in the analyzed setting. The result identifies a specific algorithmic restriction that faster finite-sum methods can avoid.
neurips-2018-breaking-the-span-assumptio.tldr: Modified SVRG and SARAH escape a gradient-span restriction and achieve provably optimal speedups in the analyzed big-data regime.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to learn representations that transfer between domains. Adversarial methods pursue this by aligning representations, but classification data can contain multiple modes that make alignment difficult. This paper argues that predictions from the classifier supply useful discriminative information for guiding that process, rather than treating domain alignment independently of what the classifier predicts.

The proposed conditional domain adversarial networks use two conditioning strategies. Multilinear conditioning captures cross-covariance between feature representations and classifier predictions, with the aim of improving class discrimination. Entropy conditioning addresses the uncertainty of those predictions to support transferability. Together, the strategies make both predicted class information and prediction uncertainty part of adversarial adaptation.

Experiments on five benchmark datasets report results exceeding the state of the art. These findings support the proposed combination in the evaluated adaptation tasks. The central methodological contribution is a framework in which the adaptation model receives structured information from the classifier, helping connect the goal of transferable features with the goal of distinguishing classes.
neurips-2018-conditional-adversarial-dom.tldr: Conditioning adversarial domain adaptation on classifier predictions and their uncertainty improves transfer results on five benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating a property of a discrete distribution usually starts with a finite sample. This paper asks whether a better estimator can make that sample as useful as a much larger one would be under the common empirical estimator. Its data amplification refers to improved estimation performance from available observations, rather than collecting additional data.

The authors construct a unified estimator that runs in linear time. For a broad class of properties and every underlying distribution, it uses 2n observations to attain the performance of the empirical estimator using n√(log n) observations. The guarantee is distribution-independent within the stated property class, making the same general approach applicable across multiple estimation tasks.

Empirical comparisons cover many properties and distributions. In most tested cases, n observations suffice to match the empirical estimator using n log n observations, a stronger amplification than the general guarantee. For essentially all properties examined, performance is comparable to the best existing property-specific estimator. These findings suggest practical benefits from a common method without requiring a separate estimator for each property.
neurips-2018-data-amplification-a-unifie.tldr: A linear-time estimator makes limited samples competitive with much larger empirical-estimation datasets across a broad class of distribution properties.

paragraphs: DeepExposure addresses exposure adjustment when different regions of a photograph need different treatment. Inspired by photographers' luminosity masks, it divides an image into sub-images using low-level features that reflect exposure variation. A policy network then learns local exposure settings sequentially, while a reward evaluates the balance of exposure across the whole image.

The method combines reinforcement learning with adversarial learning. A discriminator approximates aesthetic evaluation, and the two learning components are trained collaboratively using asynchronous deterministic policy gradients and an approximation to the generative loss. The authors also prove that using the discriminator as the value function is feasible, offering a way to simplify the architecture.

To produce the final photograph, each learned local exposure is applied to the raw input, creating several retouched versions. Exposure blending fuses these versions into one output. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in quantitative accuracy and visual results. The approach connects local adjustment decisions with global evaluation, then combines their effects through image blending.
neurips-2018-deepexposure-learning-to-ex.tldr: DeepExposure learns local exposure adjustments with reinforcement and adversarial learning, then blends retouched images to improve photographic exposure.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a low-rank approximation of a matrix while satisfying differential privacy and retaining robustness to large outliers. It measures reconstruction error using an entrywise ℓp norm. For p between one and two, excluding two, this choice is known to provide robustness to gross outliers in the data.

The target guarantee separates error into two parts: a multiplicative factor times the best achievable rank-k error, plus an additive term. For an n-by-d matrix, the proposed algorithm gives factors of approximately k² and k²(n+kd)/ε, respectively, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its running time is approximately linear in n+d with polynomial dependence on k, and its space use is O(k(n+d) log k).

The authors also study streaming versions in which matrix entries arrive in arbitrary order, with results released either at the end or continually. A related extension addresses robust private PCA by returning a rank-k projection. These results place privacy, outlier robustness, and computational resource requirements within explicit approximation guarantees.
neurips-2018-differentially-private-robu.tldr: The paper gives differentially private low-rank approximation algorithms with robust error guarantees and extensions to streaming data and PCA.

paragraphs: Active search tries to discover as many members of a target class as possible by choosing which candidates to evaluate. Scientific screening often allows several candidates to be tested simultaneously, but earlier active-search work focused on one-at-a-time selection. This paper studies how to choose batches while accounting for their effects on later search decisions.

The authors derive a Bayesian optimal batch policy and prove a lower bound on the gap between optimal sequential and batch search. This formalizes a cost of parallelization: batching changes how much feedback can inform subsequent choices. They also propose efficient batch policies inspired by sequential methods and a pruning technique that can substantially reduce computation.

Experiments compare 14 policies over varied batch sizes using citation-network, materials-science, and drug-discovery data. The observed performance gap matches the theoretical bound. Policies that consider future consequences usually significantly outperform myopic alternatives, and diversity emerges as an important design consideration. The findings connect practical batch selection with both the informational cost of batching and the value of looking ahead.
neurips-2018-efficient-nonmyopic-batch-a.tldr: The paper quantifies the cost of batch active search and develops efficient policies whose lookahead usually improves discovery in experiments.

paragraphs: A neural network trained to minimize prediction error does not necessarily learn how uncertain its predictions should be. This paper explicitly models classification uncertainty within a deterministic network. It draws on subjective logic, treating a prediction as an opinion supported by evidence learned from data.

The network outputs parameters of a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities. Its prediction therefore includes a distribution over possible probability assignments, providing a representation of uncertainty alongside class information. The network learns a function that gathers the evidence underlying these opinions. This places uncertainty directly at the prediction level, whereas Bayesian neural networks infer it indirectly through uncertainty about weights.

The authors offer a preliminary analysis of how their loss function encourages improved uncertainty estimates. They also report strong observed success in detecting out-of-distribution queries and withstanding adversarial perturbations. Those findings are empirical outcomes of the proposed method. The contribution is a way to train a deterministic classifier whose output explicitly represents evidential uncertainty, together with initial analysis and evaluation of that representation.
neurips-2018-evidential-deep-learning-to.tldr: A deterministic network predicts a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities to represent evidence and classification uncertainty explicitly.

paragraphs: Similarity search becomes challenging when datasets are large and each item has many dimensions. Many approaches reduce dimensionality to make searching cheaper. This paper explores a different representation: it raises the dimension while ensuring that the resulting data are sparse. The goal is to improve both search precision and speed through this sparse representation.

The approach has two optimization stages. First, it computes a sparse higher-dimensional representation of the supplied samples while approximately preserving their pairwise similarities. Second, it learns a lifting operator that maps the input samples as closely as possible to that representation. Separating these stages distinguishes the desired representation from the mapping used to produce it.

Both optimization problems can be solved efficiently with the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. The authors report significantly improved results in empirical evaluations and see potential for practical similarity-search applications. The finding supports sparse dimensional expansion as a useful design choice: a representation's number of dimensions is considered together with its sparsity and how well it retains similarities.
neurips-2018-fast-similarity-search-via-.tldr: Optimal sparse lifting expands data into a sparse higher-dimensional space that approximately preserves similarities and improves search results empirically.

paragraphs: FastRNN and FastGRNN address a practical tension in recurrent neural networks: improving training accuracy can increase model size and prediction costs. Those costs matter for real-time applications and devices with very little memory. The paper develops recurrent architectures intended to retain accuracy while reducing the resources required for prediction.

FastRNN adds a residual connection using only two extra scalar parameters, without explicitly restricting the singular values of the state-transition matrix. FastGRNN extends this connection into a gate while reusing the recurrent network's matrices. The authors report accuracy matching state-of-the-art gated recurrent networks with models two to four times smaller.

Further enforcing low rank, sparsity, and quantization produces accurate FastGRNN models up to 35 times smaller than leading gated and unitary alternatives. A one-kilobyte model recognizes the Hey Cortana wakeword, and the architecture is deployed on microcontrollers too small to store other recurrent models. These results connect architectural parameter reuse with additional compression techniques and a concrete deployment on severely constrained hardware.
neurips-2018-fastgrnn-a-fast-accurate-st.tldr: FastGRNN reuses recurrent matrices for gating and combines compression techniques to deliver accurate models small enough for constrained microcontrollers.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can demand too much storage and computation for mobile devices. Pruning addresses this by removing parameters that contribute little to performance. This paper focuses on spatial redundancy within convolutional filters: correlations among filter values suggest that the frequency domain may offer a useful place to identify and remove redundant information.

The proposed scheme dynamically prunes frequency-domain coefficients at each iteration. It treats frequency bands differently because they differ in their importance to accuracy. The method therefore combines a change in representation with an adaptive pruning process, using spatial correlations to guide compression rather than treating all frequency components alike.

Experiments report substantial improvements over earlier spatial-domain pruning methods. For ResNet-110, the abstract reports 8.4-fold compression and a theoretical 9.2-fold inference speedup, with accuracy above the reference model on the dataset it calls CIFAR-110. The speedup is explicitly theoretical. The reported result shows that frequency-based pruning can combine strong compression with preserved or improved accuracy in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2018-frequency-domain-dynamic-pr.tldr: Dynamic frequency-domain pruning exploits filter correlations, reporting 8.4-fold compression and a theoretical 9.2-fold speedup for ResNet-110.

paragraphs: Asynchronous Gibbs sampling had already been shown to estimate probabilities involving small groups of variables accurately under Dobrushin's condition. This paper asks whether it can also estimate expectations of functions involving every variable in a graphical model. The distinction matters because accuracy for local events does not itself settle accuracy for global quantities.

Under the same condition, the authors couple sequential and asynchronous samplers so that their samples differ in an expected O(τ log n) coordinates, where n counts variables and τ measures asynchronicity. They obtain related bounds for constant powers of this Hamming distance. Consequently, functions satisfying the stated Lipschitz regularity have estimation bias that grows logarithmically with n.

The analysis also examines polynomial functions beyond this Lipschitz argument. Using concentration results, the authors show that the bias caused by asynchronicity is smaller in order than the standard deviation already present under the true model. Multiprocessor experiments illustrate the theory. The results establish conditional accuracy guarantees for broader, global quantities while explicitly relating asynchronous error to ordinary statistical variation.
neurips-2018-hogwild-gibbs-can-be-panacc.tldr: Under Dobrushin's condition, asynchronous Gibbs sampling has controlled bias for broad classes of functions involving all model variables.

paragraphs: Networks trained on the same task can develop representations with very different structures, making direct comparisons difficult. This paper develops projection-weighted canonical correlation analysis, building on SVCCA, to study those representations. The improved method distinguishes signal from noise and provides a tool for comparing networks and tracking changes during training.

Applied to convolutional networks, the method reveals that networks which generalize converge to more similar representations than networks which memorize. Wider networks also converge to more similar solutions than narrower ones. Networks with identical topology but different learning rates form distinct clusters of representations, showing that the training configuration can correspond to substantial representational differences.

The authors additionally examine recurrent networks across training and across positions in a sequence. They find bottom-up convergence during training and substantial hidden-state variation along a sequence, even after accounting for linear transformations. Together, these findings show how representation comparisons can expose differences associated with generalization, width, learning rate, and temporal processing, extending analysis beyond a network's final predictions.
neurips-2018-insights-on-representationa.tldr: Projection-weighted CCA reveals how neural representations differ with generalization, width, learning rate, training progress, and sequence position.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult to guide safely when the reward function is hard to specify. This paper proposes a framework that uses demonstrations from expert policies to inform the agent's behavior. Access to those demonstrations is an explicit premise: the expert provides information that helps constrain which rewards are consistent with what the agent knows.

The theoretical framework lets the agent optimize over this space of consistent rewards. This connects policy learning to uncertainty about the objective itself. The authors present two approaches to the resulting optimization problem: an exact method based on ellipsoids and another method inspired by follow-the-perturbed-leader.

Experiments demonstrate the algorithm in both discrete and continuous problems. The trained agent avoids states with potentially negative effects while imitating expert behavior in other states. These outcomes illustrate how expert guidance can support caution in uncertain situations while retaining imitation elsewhere. The contribution combines a reward-based theoretical formulation, two optimization methods, and demonstrations of the resulting behavior across both kinds of problem.
neurips-2018-learning-safe-policies-with.tldr: Expert demonstrations constrain plausible rewards, enabling a learning framework that avoids potentially harmful states in discrete and continuous experiments.

paragraphs: A generative model learning new categories sequentially can lose the ability to generate categories it learned earlier. This paper investigates that problem in generative adversarial networks. The authors first demonstrate that sequential fine-tuning leads to forgetting, extending a concern often studied in discriminative models to the quality of generated images.

Their solution, Memory Replay GANs, is a conditional GAN framework with a generator that provides memory replays. They study two ways to use those replays: joint training with replay and replay alignment. In both cases, replay supplies a mechanism for retaining earlier generative behavior while the model learns additional categories.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations on MNIST, SVHN, and LSUN show that the approach produces competitive images while significantly reducing forgetting of previous categories. The stated outcome is mitigation rather than complete elimination of forgetting. The work establishes sequential category learning as a challenge for image generation and demonstrates that incorporating generated replays can help preserve earlier capabilities as the model's category repertoire grows.
neurips-2018-memory-replay-gans-learning.tldr: Memory Replay GANs use generated replays to learn new image categories while substantially reducing forgetting of earlier categories.

paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private learning methods that can use a generic non-private learner, assuming access to a limited amount of unlabeled public data. Its first task is to answer an online sequence of classification queries using a private training set. Separate classifiers are trained on disjoint portions of that set, and their votes are combined privately.

The aggregation mechanism combines distance to instability with the sparse-vector technique to conserve the privacy budget. If the underlying learner has error at most α, the construction can, in some cases, answer at least 1/α times as many queries as a straightforward use of advanced composition would imply. This improvement is conditional, rather than a uniform gain for every setting.

The authors then use knowledge transfer to produce a private classifier that can answer unlimited subsequent queries. They establish sample-complexity upper bounds in the PAC framework for both realizable and non-realizable cases. As in non-private learning, these bounds are characterized by the concept class's VC dimension, connecting model-independent privacy mechanisms with established measures of learning complexity.
neurips-2018-model-agnostic-private-lear.tldr: Private aggregation and knowledge transfer turn generic learners into privacy-preserving query systems and classifiers, given limited unlabeled public data.

paragraphs: Estimating an individual's treatment effect from observational data is difficult because the counterfactual outcome is missing and treatment selection can introduce bias. Existing methods described in the paper emphasize balancing the distributions of treated and control groups. The authors argue that this leaves out useful information about similarities among nearby examples.

The proposed SITE method learns a deep representation that both preserves local similarity and balances the two groups' distributions. It focuses on several difficult examples within each mini-batch to pursue these objectives together. The approach therefore incorporates relationships among individual samples alongside the broader comparison between treated and untreated populations.

Experiments on synthetic data and three real-world datasets report advantages over state-of-the-art individual treatment-effect estimators. These findings support combining local similarity preservation with distribution balancing in the tested settings. The contribution is a representation-learning method that treats both as useful parts of treatment-effect estimation, addressing information that group-level balancing alone can overlook without claiming that observational estimation's underlying difficulties disappear.
neurips-2018-representation-learning-for.tldr: SITE combines local similarity preservation with treated-control distribution balancing to improve individual treatment-effect estimation in experiments.

paragraphs: Expectation-Maximization learns models with latent variables, but standard batch EM needs the entire dataset at every expectation step. Stochastic EM reduces that cost through stochastic approximation. Its tradeoffs include slower asymptotic convergence and a decreasing step-size schedule that can be difficult to tune, creating a tension between cheaper updates and the progress those updates achieve.

The paper introduces variance-reduced stochastic EM, inspired by variance-reduction methods for stochastic gradient descent. The authors show that it attains the same exponential asymptotic convergence rate as batch EM. It achieves that rate with a constant step size, reducing the need to design a sequence of progressively smaller steps.

Experiments compare the method with batch EM, ordinary stochastic EM, and other algorithms on Gaussian mixture models and probabilistic latent semantic analysis. The proposed method converges significantly faster in those comparisons. The contribution thus combines a convergence-rate result with a simpler step-size requirement and empirical evidence of faster learning on two latent-variable modeling tasks.
neurips-2018-stochastic-expectation-maxi.tldr: Variance-reduced stochastic EM matches batch EM's exponential asymptotic convergence rate with a constant step size and converges faster in reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether samples from an unknown discrete distribution can establish membership in a specified family. The testing goal is to distinguish, with high probability, a distribution inside the family from one at least ε away from every member in total variation distance. This formulation asks for a reliable distinction between membership and substantial departure.

The authors develop a general technique based on the Fourier transform. It applies to distribution families whose Fourier spectra have a particular approximate sparsity property. That structural condition is central: it identifies the families for which the framework can yield efficient tests, rather than asserting a method for every possible family.

Applications cover sums of independent integer random variables, Poisson multinomial distributions, and discrete log-concave distributions. The resulting testers are computationally efficient and nearly optimal in sample use. For the first two families, the paper provides the first nontrivial testers, extending earlier Poisson-binomial testing work. For discrete log-concave distributions, it improves both sample and time complexity over previous methods.
neurips-2018-testing-for-families-of-dis.tldr: Approximate sparsity in the Fourier domain enables efficient, nearly sample-optimal membership tests for several important discrete distribution families.

paragraphs: The paper combines adversarial and autoregressive modeling for text generation. Its procedure first generates a high-level sentence outline and then produces words one at a time. Each word depends on both that outline and the preceding outputs, giving the sequential generator a source of sentence-level conditioning throughout generation.

The outlines are representations in a latent space defined by general-purpose sentence encoders. An adversarial model learns to approximate the distribution of sentences in that space. This separates the task of producing informative sentence-level guidance from the task of turning that guidance into a sequence of words, while connecting the two through conditioning.

Quantitative evaluations suggest that generated outlines guide the autoregressive model toward realistic text comparable to maximum-likelihood-trained language models, even with high-temperature multinomial sampling. Qualitative results also show natural-looking sentences and interpolations. These findings support the usefulness of learned latent outlines as guidance for word-by-word generation, with the quantitative comparison presented as evidence from the evaluated settings.
neurips-2018-towards-text-generation-wit.tldr: Adversarially generated latent sentence outlines guide an autoregressive model toward realistic text, including under high-temperature sampling in evaluations.
